[USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"Minutes"] from the US Federal Reserve's September monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank unanimously approved its first interest rate hike since July 2023, revealed divisions over the rationale of the increase. Some participants saw a hike as necessary to keep the impact of energy price shocks at bay, while others felt the increase was necessary to curb demand-driven inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in a 17.2% likelihood that the Fed will implement a second consecutive rate hike at the conclusion of its October meeting, down from 37.6% a week ago, per CME's FedWatch tool. "The market’s Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data," Martin said. "There's still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn't necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that's what the market is telling you; October will be a pause." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 341.11 points, or 0.66%, to 51,180.17, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 17.18 points, or 0.22%, to 7,801.75 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 61.19 points, or 0.22%, to 27,538.69. Among the 11 sectors in the S&P 500, industrials (.SPLRCI) suffered the steepest percentage drop, while healthcare stocks (.SPXHC) led the gainers. Following the upward march of benchmark Treasury yields, the 30-year fixed [USN:L1N45T0EH TEXT:"mortgage rate"] surged last week to a near three-year high, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Housing (.HGX) and homebuilders (.SPCOMHOME) slipped 2.3% and 2.9%, respectively. Chip stocks (.SOX) , which have soared over 80% so far this year, dropped 1.2%. [USN:L6N45S1CR TEXT:"SpaceX"] (SPCX.O) lost 2.5% following media reports that Elon Musk's aerospace firm was seeking $40 billion in financing to fund purchases of Nvidia chips. Next week, third-quarter reporting season is expected to begin in earnest with a spate of high-profile financial firms expected to post results. Investors are likely to scrutinize the extent to which massive expenditures on AI technology are beginning to show results, while also watching for clues regarding the health of the US consumer at a time of mounting inflationary pressures. Analysts currently expect year-on-year S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-through-September period, according to LSEG. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.34-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 115 new highs and 497 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 1,421 stocks rose and 3,371 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.37-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 9 new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 32 new highs and 250 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.21 billion shares, compared with the 17.57 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: Microsoft brings more AI to PCs as it challenges Apple
item.description: Microsoft unveiled on Wednesday an AI coding model that can run directly on personal computers and new security technology to prevent AI agents from accessing data without permission, challenging Apple's push to bring more AI into personal devices.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) unveiled on Wednesday an AI coding model that can run directly on personal computers and new security technology to prevent AI agents from accessing data without permission, challenging Apple's (AAPL.O) push to bring more AI into personal devices. The software company also presented at the event in San Francisco a high-powered Surface laptop called Ultra powered by Nvidia's (NVDA.O) [USN:L6N42909E TEXT:"RTX Spark chips"]. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft is seeking to turn Windows into a platform for AI agents to handle tasks such as writing computer code or tackling complex business projects on desktops and laptops. For Microsoft, the move represents a bet that some work that currently happens in its costly Azure cloud computing data centers can shift to high-powered Windows machines in businesses and homes, a market where the firm retains a stronghold — and where its customers foot the hardware bills. It is a market opportunity rival [USN:L6N45D0ZZ TEXT:"Apple is also chasing"] with new Mac computers. For Nvidia, cracking the Windows PC market could help it go after one of the last major markets dominated by Intel (INTC.O) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O) . As a guardrail against increasingly autonomous AI agents that have created security risks, Microsoft said it was releasing Microsoft Execution Containers, a tool to prevent agents from accessing data and doing unauthorized tasks when running on a laptop or desktop machine. Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia will use the tools, said Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president for Windows and devices. “We needed to make the desktop the most secure place for agents to execute,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said. Davuluri said new tools would let IT departments set rules for agents and the Windows operating system would enforce those rules on each employee’s machine. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who joined Nadella on stage, said Microsoft’s new execution container technology, which goes by MXC for short, "is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed.” “Without it, (agents are) a complete nonstarter,” he said. Nvidia is [USN:L6N45K077 TEXT:"trying to prevent"] a repeat of the hack of AI hub Hugging Face, while Apple is looking to [USN:L6N45O14K TEXT:"tighten up the process"] for giving AI agents full access to a Mac computer's hard drive. AI MOVES TO THE PC Microsoft also unveiled AI models that previously required cloud access but can now run locally on high-powered Windows desktops and laptops, including Nvidia's open-source Nemotron model. Davuluri said a version of Chinese AI firm DeepSeek's V4 model can run on machines with at least 60 gigabytes of memory and outperform OpenAI's GPT-5 on some coding and reasoning tasks. Microsoft is taking a similar approach with its own Copilot AI assistant, splitting tasks between the cloud and individual laptops. “Copilot will still use the cloud for the hardest tasks, but for times when cost or privacy matter more, it can delegate down to local models that run directly on your computer,” said Microsoft’s Copilot chief Jacob Andreou. Davuluri also said Meta's (META.O) Muse personal assistant will come to Windows devices as a native app, using some of Microsoft’s new security tools, and that OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent system, can also work with those security tools. PRICE BARRIER One of the key challenges Microsoft and Nvidia face is the steep pricing of these devices after a memory-chip crunch drove up costs. The new Surface Laptop Ultra will start at $2,599 and rise to $5,899 for a model with a 20-core processor, 128 gigabytes of memory and one terabyte of storage. Apple's MacBook Pro with a 40-core graphics chip, 128 GB of memory and two TB of storage costs $6,700, although the machines are not directly comparable. Microsoft's entry-level Ultra costs more than Apple's $1,999 base MacBook Pro, but comes with 24 GB of memory compared with 16 GB on Apple's entry-level model. When Microsoft originally pitched the idea of running AI tasks on PCs two years ago to save costs, the laptops were mostly priced below $2,000, but Nvidia increased the price of an AI desktop machine called the DGX Spark by about 75% since its launch to $6,950 amid rising memory costs. Two years ago, "the software wasn't ready, but the hardware was. Now the software is ready and the hardware is too expensive to actually run it locally," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "So it's becoming this thing where only the people who have the budget can really afford to run AI locally."

item.title: Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
item.description: Reuters reviewed voting records, public statements and campaign materials.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Layne, David Morgan
item.content:encoded: Two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him, a Reuters review found, revealing a widespread effort to distance themselves from the president as his unpopularity threatens the party's hold on Congress. The review of voting records, public statements and campaign materials found candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races seeking some distance from Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections . The candidates have largely criticized or diverged from Trump on individual issues rather than repudiated his broader agenda. The findings suggest an effort to attract independent voters while avoiding a direct break with their party leader. Policy differences were the most common point of divergence, appearing in 23 of the 62 races. In 12 contests, the split centered on the Iran conflict, with vulnerable Republicans either voting to curb Trump's war powers or calling publicly for an end to the fighting that has raised gas prices and squeezed household budgets. Data centers are among the issues dividing Trump and some Republican candidates. Reuters identified three candidates in competitive races who have criticized or sought to slow such projects despite the president's support for faster development. The shift is notable because Trump has spent the past decade remaking the Republican Party in his own image and has been swift to punish lawmakers and candidates who defied him through primary challenges, personal attacks or public pressure to fall into line. In response to questions about the Reuters findings, White House spokesman Davis Ingle pointed to the administration's accomplishments and said Trump was "the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator" for the party. While news organizations have highlighted individual cases of distancing, the Reuters review is the first to systematically measure the trend across competitive races that will decide whether Republicans retain control of either or both chambers of Congress. A new [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"] underscored the challenge facing Republicans: Trump's approval rating remained stuck at a career-low 32%, while registered voters favored Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ahead of the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%. CREATING DISTANCE FROM TRUMP Reuters also found a broad effort to play down ties: A dozen candidates removed his name, image or endorsements from campaign websites, most after securing their party's nomination. Others acted in subtler ways, skipping his events or declining to say whether he should campaign on their behalf. Direct criticism was relatively rare, underscoring Trump's dominance of the Republican Party and the risks candidates face in openly challenging a president who still commands the loyalty of many ardent supporters. Candidates distancing themselves from an unpopular president before an election is not unusual. Democrats employed similar tactics in the 2014 and 2022 elections. While Reuters did not conduct a comparable review of competitive races in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, analysts said Trump has rarely faced such widespread pushback by vulnerable Republican candidates. "(Candidates) are reflecting voter attitudes in these races," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "If (voters) are not with Trump, then they need to show a break." Privately, campaign advisers told Reuters that candidates needed to dial back ties to Trump to attract independent voters. Publicly, they dismissed criticism of the repositioning. BALANCING ACT Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who faces a tough challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, exemplifies the 11 candidates identified by Reuters who broke with Trump on one policy issue while backing him on everything else. The balancing act was on display this week when Ricketts, who criticized Trump's plan to expand beef imports, joined the president at a Nebraska rally. "President Trump, I have been fighting for you in Washington," Ricketts told the crowd. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican in one of the country's most competitive House races in Iowa, has also shown a growing willingness to break with the administration. She was among 12 candidates identified by Reuters who split with Trump on multiple issues, criticizing his beef-import policy and later voting to limit his war powers in Iran after previously opposing similar measures. Yet, less than two weeks after her war-powers vote, Miller-Meeks joined Trump at the White House to announce a major steel plant investment in Iowa. "It is a balancing act," said Republican consultant Jeanette Hoffman, adding that candidates are trying to capitalize on the administration’s successes while creating some distance from Trump because of “how toxic the Trump brand is at the moment.” SCRUBBING TRUMP REFERENCES As Republicans in competitive races seek to expand their appeal beyond Trump's core supporters, some candidates have begun dialing back public displays of loyalty to the president. Mike Beltran, a former Florida state representative running against Democratic US Representative Kathy Castor, is among candidates who have scrubbed prominent references to Trump from their campaign websites. In August, his homepage featured a photo of Trump and said he stood with the president, according to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive website. Now Beltran's homepage shows only him and his family and makes no mention of Trump. Beltran's campaign had no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment. Representative Mike Lawler of New York, facing one of the most competitive US House races, embodies the balancing act confronting many Republicans in battleground districts: staying close to Trump while demonstrating independence from him. Lawler has highlighted breaks with Trump on issues including temporary legal protections for Haitian immigrants and a Trump-backed proposal to restore Turkey's access to F-35 fighter jets. His campaign manager Ciro Riccardi said Lawler acts on behalf of his constituency regardless of a president's stance. Lawler acknowledged the disagreements in a speech to Trump supporters at the Republican midterm convention in September, saying, "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree. And that's OK."

item.title: AI companies run virtual drug trials, aim to improve success of human studies
item.description: Novartis’ experimental del-desiran for a rare type of muscular dystrophy was expected to be a winner, with the Swiss company's CEO predicting annual peak sales of $5 billion. When a late-stage trial missed its goal last month, shares fell 11%, erasing $30 billion in market value.
item.dc:creator: Deena Beasley
item.content:encoded: Novartis’ (NOVN.S) experimental del-desiran for a rare type of muscular dystrophy was expected to be a winner, with the Swiss company's CEO predicting annual peak sales of $5 billion. When a [USN:L8N45006F TEXT:"late-stage trial"] missed its goal last month, shares fell 11%, erasing $30 billion in market value. AI start-up BioinvestGPT was not surprised. In July, it ran a simulated trial to measure how virtual patients would respond to del-desiran and predicted an insignificant clinical benefit. It and other artificial intelligence companies say they are working with some drugmakers on virtual trials to boost the odds an experimental medicine will prove safe and effective when used by actual patients in an expensive traditional clinical trial. The global biopharmaceutical industry spends some $140 billion a year on human clinical testing, but only around 12% of drug candidates are approved by regulators — a rate that has changed little in decades. AI firms say simulations are being used to identify which pharmaceutical programs are worth moving forward and to assess the value of acquisition targets. As AI tools get better at flagging clinical risks, they say unexpected trial failures may become less frequent. Human clinical trials typically start with small Phase 1 studies primarily to gauge safety, followed by mid-stage Phase 2 and the large Phase 3 trials required by regulators that also assess efficacy. The process takes years, compared with a month or less for some AI simulations. "We shouldn't only ask how to run trials faster. We should ask how to run fewer trials that are going to fail," said Francisco Beca, chief medical officer at QuantHealth, an AI clinical trial simulation platform headquartered in Tel Aviv. Investment in AI drug discovery more than doubled to $8.4 billion in 2025 compared to 2023, according to a recent report from McKinsey . It said spending is currently focused where the technology works best today, particularly molecule design, rather than the industry's major bottlenecks, such as proving a drug will work as intended through lengthy trials. Pharma companies are "dipping their toes" into AI trial modeling, said McKinsey partner Alex Devereson. They are using different types of the technology, internally or with partners, to do things like assess drug candidates before committing capital to a program, he said. US health regulators last week announced a set of initiatives aimed at speeding drug trials. If successful, the program could help create a path for predictive AI to be used in clinical development, a federal health official said. FIVE OUT OF SIX CORRECT Copenhagen-based BioinvestGPT in July shared with Reuters its detailed analyses of the likely outcome of several high-profile drug trials before the results were known and has so far been correct in five of six. They include the negative result for del-desiran, success for Moderna (MRNA.O) and Merck's (MRK.N) [USN:L1N44F0SC TEXT:"melanoma vaccine"], a weak clinical benefit for AstraZeneca (AZN.L) and Ionis' (IONS.O) heart drug [USN:L6N43B0BH TEXT:"Wainua"], the first failed trial for Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) heart drug [USN:L4N43X1AC TEXT:"ziltivekimab"], and success for [USN:L4N45R0K6 TEXT:"Vaxcyte's"] (PCVX.O) pneumococcal vaccine. The fundamental goal of the pharma industry is proof of a superior clinical benefit compared to the standard of care, said Bragi Lovetrue, who co-founded BioinvestGPT with his wife Idonae Lovetrue in 2024. The AI platform uses DNA sequencing to simulate a human body matching the eligibility criteria for a specific clinical trial. A virtual trial is then done using a model of the test drug. "We can pinpoint the reason why a drug is effective and safe, and in many cases, why not," Lovetrue said. The simulations are not always right. The predictive AI forecast positive results for Novartis' [USN:L4N44W1D6 TEXT:"pelacarsen"], which lowers blood levels of a cholesterol-carrier called lipoprotein(a). Novartis in September said the drug did not cut the risk of a major heart attack or stroke in patients with a genetic risk factor in a late-stage trial. A subsequent analysis showed "we got the mechanism wrong," by not accounting for genetically set variations in the size of the lipoprotein, Lovetrue said. QuantHealth, which uses real-world data and AI to simulate patient-level responses to therapies, has published its simulations of ulcerative colitis and cholesterol drug trials. BIOGEN, TAKEDA TRIALS PREDICTED TO FAIL BioinvestGPT has done predictions for a wide range of trials. For anticipated trial results expected before year-end, the AI company predicts failure for two Phase 3 trials of Biogen's (BIIB.O) litifilimab in the most common type of lupus, as well as for Phase 2 studies of Japanese drugmaker Takeda's (4502.T) zasocitinib in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. The AI model shows that both drugs are "suboptimal" for those specific trial populations. Biogen's drug, which targets an immune cell receptor called BDCA2, is also being studied in a [USN:L4N45O11Z TEXT:"different type"] of lupus. Takeda filed recently for US approval of zasocitinib, which blocks an enzyme called tyrosine kinase 2, in plaque psoriasis and has a Phase 3 trial in psoriatic arthritis. Takeda research chief Andy Plump said TYK2 was identified as a target by analyzing human genetics, while machine learning was used to optimize and "polish" the structure of the daily pill. "I have immense confidence in this mechanism," Plump said. "I don't think we are near being able to use tools like AI to make definitive predictions." Diana Gallagher, Biogen's head of clinical development for multiple sclerosis, immunology and Alzheimer's, said the company uses "every tool available to us," including AI. She said only two biologic drugs have been approved for lupus and AI algorithms that rely on historical data could be prone to predicting a negative result. QuantHealth's Beca and other experts said human trials will always be necessary, but AI simulations can be valuable when assessing the potential of an experimental drug. "Is it still ethical in 2026 to expose patients to a trial that most likely will fail?" he said. "With the advancement of this (AI) technology, come 2027, 2028, or 2029, probably the answer is going to be that it no longer is."

item.title: US bonds selloff eases, yields off highs, after strong 10-year note auction
item.description: US Treasuries rose in afternoon trading on Wednesday, with yields backing away from their highs as oil prices fell and a strong $39 billion auction of 10-year notes reassured investors that demand for long-term government debt remained intact despite recent market volatility.
item.dc:creator: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
item.content:encoded: US Treasuries rose in afternoon trading on Wednesday, with yields backing away from their highs as oil prices fell and a strong $39 billion auction of 10-year notes reassured investors that demand for long-term government debt remained intact despite recent market volatility. US government debt earlier came under renewed selling pressure, driving yields on the benchmark 10-year note and 30-year bond to fresh 24-year highs as oil prices jumped above $100. That re-ignited worries that inflation may prove more stubborn than expected. Rising yields mean Treasury debt prices were higher. A strong $39 billion sale of 10-year notes sparked buying across the Treasury market, analysts said. Some investors had feared weak demand given persistent bearish sentiment toward longer-dated Treasuries in recent months, driven in part by renewed concerns over rising fiscal deficits. "It was a good auction given how much the 10-year has sold off, and it's good to see buyers step in," said Vinny Bleau, director of fixed income research at Raymond James in Memphis. "You can be afraid of it (the selloff), or you can take advantage of it." The drop in oil prices also helped yields drift lower from their highs after the International Energy Agency [USN:L6N45T0GQ TEXT:"agreed to speed up"] a release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel in a bid to curb record high fuel prices. Brent crude fell 0.5% to $100.09 per barrel, while US crude slid 1.1% to $88.32 per barrel. In afternoon trading, the benchmark 10-year yield was up 1.3 basis points (bps) to 5.284% after hitting a 24-year peak of 5.364% earlier. US 30-year yields also touched a 24-year high and were last 2.8 bps higher at 5.669% . On the shorter end of the curve, US 2-year yields, which reflect interest rate expectations, were down 2.3 bps at 4.768% . SPACEX FACTOR US debt was also earlier undermined by reports that Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX.O) , a rockets-to-AI firm, was [USN:L6N45S1CR TEXT:"seeking $40 billion in financing"] to fund purchases of Nvidia chips. The Financial Times reported that SpaceX is looking to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt for the chip order. If SpaceX enters the investment-grade bond market, it could revive concerns that large-scale corporate borrowing is competing with long-dated US Treasuries for investor capital, analysts said. "The amount of demand of private sector borrowing, particularly for long paper ... has grown so significantly that it has created this crowding-out effect or competition for capital," said Thomas Urano, co-chief investment officer at Sage Advisory in Austin. The 10-year Treasury auction, meanwhile, went down smoothly, pricing at [USN:AQN2MN6IG TEXT:"5.3%"], lower than the expected rate at the bid deadline, suggesting that investors did not need a premium to take down the benchmark debt. The bid-to-cover ratio, a measure of demand, was 2.77, above the six-auction average of 2.54. Primary dealers were left with just 2.5% of the offering, their smallest share since the aftermath of the global financial crisis, suggesting investor demand was strong enough that dealers were not required to absorb much of the issue. 'CALMED THE NERVES' "The strong stop through and high end-user demand may have calmed the nerves of some investors thinking that there would be no demand given the rise in yields," said Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US rates strategy at TD Securities. "On the contrary, we think higher yields are prompting investors to dip their toes even as they worry about recent volatility." Minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting were also released on Wednesday, [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"with policymakers divided"] over the rationale for raising interest rates. "Some participants" saw a hike as needed to keep the impact of energy and other price shocks at bay, but a more hawkish core viewed it as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation, the minutes showed. Elsewhere in the Treasury market, the yield curve steepened on Wednesday with the spread between two-year and 10-year yields widening to 52.2 bps from 48.1 bps. The curve hit 53.7 bps, its steepest level since mid-August after long-dated yields rose more sharply than shorter-dated ones, a move known as a bear steepener. A bear steepener reflects a pickup in inflation expectations.

item.title: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
item.description: Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Osborn, Jennifer Rigby
item.content:encoded: Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a [USN:L1N45S0CY TEXT:"plague institute worker"] there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death. Russian authorities say [USN:L1N45R0VI TEXT:"the 28-year-old laboratory worker"] died last Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in [USN:L1N45S0CY TEXT:"a case that has prompted international concern"], including from US President Donald Trump. Around 200 people were initially placed in quarantine. Asked on Wednesday whether the death was caused by a bioweapon, Trump told reporters: "Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." He said Russia was not saying much about the situation but "they do say they have it very much under control," adding he had set up a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. "They're sharing (information) a little bit with our people. We expect them to share it a lot with our people," said Trump, speaking in the Oval Office. Global health officials - as well as the world's media - have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined. US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz said at an event the agency was prepared to monitor and screen travelers although the risk to the US was [USN:L4N45T1BB TEXT:"extremely low"]. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, based on what had been made known, but told a press conference on Wednesday it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health watchdog, said on Wednesday it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO. [USN:L8N45S0R0 TEXT:"No cases of plague had been detected"] among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens. It said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had therefore been "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked". It did not say, however, what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how she fell ill. WHO CALLS FOR MORE INFORMATION Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO in Geneva, said on Wednesday his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened. "We would like more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, and if this individual didn't die from plague, then how did she die?" Maria Van Kerkhove, director of the WHO's department of epidemic and pandemic management, told a virtual press conference. Tedros said the WHO had offered assistance to Russia and also repeated a request for Russia to verify "media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause". KREMLIN CRITICISES 'FALSE INFORMATION' IN MEDIA The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures. When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening. "There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov. He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on Wednesday about the WHO's questions. EXACT CAUSE OF DEATH REMAINS UNKNOWN Some Western media outlets have reported — citing unnamed "Russian media" — that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague. Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making — without evidence — such assertions. After the press conference, the WHO sent Reuters a link to a story about a potential second case by the Russian media organization starhit.ru, a celebrity gossip outlet, and a follow-up from British newspaper the Daily Mail. Tedros said it was important to be transparent based on the lessons from COVID, adding, "We don't have any mandate actually to see whether this media is credible or not." Russia has not formally responded to the reports about a second person dying, Tedros said, adding that he had heard only informally that Russia had denied those reports. Tedros' call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident. Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19.

item.title: IEA to accelerate oil reserve release, says 100 million barrels still to come
item.description: The International Energy Agency agreed on Wednesday to accelerate the release of oil stocks and to prioritise diesel supplies under a plan launched in March, as governments seek to tackle record fuel prices and supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Kate Abnett, Holger Hansen
item.content:encoded: The International Energy Agency agreed on Wednesday to accelerate the release of oil stocks and to prioritise diesel supplies under a plan launched in March, as governments seek to tackle record fuel prices and supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have damaged refineries and disrupted tanker traffic, helping drive diesel prices to record highs in many markets and turning the fuel into a major political and economic concern worldwide. The IEA said completing previously announced releases as quickly as possible could bring around 100 million barrels to market, although analysts and some governments said the figure did not necessarily represent a fresh intervention of that size. The statement from the IEA, which advises industrialised countries, followed an agreement by G7 countries [USN:L6N45O0G5 TEXT:"on Friday"] to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel, which raised expectations of additional oil stock releases. The G7 move came after President Donald Trump warned he might ban US diesel exports if they did not put more of the fuel into the market. The IEA, which coordinates emergency oil stockpiles among industrialised countries, launched a 400-million-barrel release programme in March to counter shortages and rising prices caused by the Iran war, although not all of those volumes have yet reached the market. "Member governments expressed support for accelerating the oil stock releases announced in the Collective Action of March 2026 with a view to completing them as soon as possible," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in the statement. "IEA members also supported the prioritisation of the release of diesel stocks, to the extent possible, given the current tightness in diesel markets." The IEA said about 100 million barrels pledged under the March initiative have yet to reach the market. The IEA did not specify how much diesel and how much crude oil will be released. In reaction to the IEA comment, the European Union member states agreed the planned oil releases must be done within the amount approved in March, a spokesperson for the European Commission said on Wednesday. IEA members are scheduled to assess and review the plans at a board meeting next week, the statement said. The G7 includes EU members France, Germany and Italy along with the US, UK, Japan and Canada. EXTENT OF NEW VOLUME NOT CLEAR Before the IEA statement, JPMorgan analysts said Friday's announcement appeared largely to accelerate deliveries already pledged under the March programme rather than signal a fresh intervention. "Our interpretation of the press release is that the headline 100 million barrels does not represent 100 million barrels of new intervention," the bank said in a report. Germany's [USN:SPN45A00B TEXT:"Economy Ministry"] said it was working to approve releases from reserves under the March plan but gave no indication of any new volume. "Germany will participate in the further release of the volume already determined by the IEA in March," the ministry said in a statement. IEA member governments still have publicly held emergency oil stocks equivalent to around 1.1 billion barrels, including over 200 million barrels of diesel, the IEA's statement said.

item.title: Gold slides to two-month low as robust dollar, yields add pressure
item.description: Gold prices slid to a two-month low on Wednesday, as a stronger dollar and elevated US Treasury yields reduced the appeal of the non-yielding metal.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sinha
item.content:encoded: Gold prices slid to a two-month low on Wednesday, as a stronger dollar and elevated US Treasury yields reduced the appeal of the non-yielding metal. Spot gold fell 1.2% to $4,113.89 per ounce by 2:12 p.m. EDT (1812 GMT), touching its lowest level since August 5. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1.1% lower at $4,140.70. The US dollar index (.DXY) climbed 0.4%, making greenback-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies, and 10-year US Treasury yields were at an over two-decade high. Markets are largely expecting the US Federal Reserve to keep interest rates on hold later this month, but are still pricing in an 85% chance of a December increase, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "I think the message is rates are going to continue to be higher for longer, and that's keeping yields and the dollar underpinned," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals. Kansas City Fed President [USN:S0N3XI00P TEXT:"Jeff Schmid"] said curbing inflation may require further rate hikes. San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N45S13A TEXT:"Mary Daly"] also said the policy path would depend on whether inflationary pressures continue. Higher interest rates diminish the attractiveness of non-yielding gold. Fed policymakers were [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"divided"] last month over the rationale for raising interest rates, with "some participants" seeing a hike as needed to keep the impact of energy and other price shocks at bay, but a more hawkish core viewing it as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation. Meanwhile, [USN:L1N45T01W TEXT:"China's central bank"] stepped up its gold purchases in September, extending its buying streak to a 23rd consecutive month, official data showed. "Official gold demand is the main supporting factor. I think we could see one more test to the downside, perhaps as low as $4,000, and then a recovery into year-end with potential to reach $4,400," Grant added. Spot silver eased 3% to $59.86 per ounce, platinum fell 3.9% to $1,635.04, and palladium lost 4% to $1,125.70.

item.title: At least 25 killed in Ukraine, Zelenskiy condemns one of Russia's most 'vile strikes'
item.description: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, killing at least 25 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash, Vladyslav Smilianets
item.content:encoded: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, killing at least 25 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure. The heaviest death toll was in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-storey residential building. Zelenskiy said 19 people died in the attack, including five children. Zelenskiy said 25 people had been killed in the strikes throughout the country, with 100 injured. Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi put the death toll at 28. The president noted that the attacks coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday. "This is the kind of birthday present that Putin gave himself: the killing of children, the killing of people," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address. In earlier online comments, Zelenskiy said civilians had also been killed in the capital Kyiv and in the central cities of Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack. In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight - many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions - and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said. "The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes." In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 survivors as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said. "There's a lot of destruction, especially in the town centre," said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying. BIG JUMP IN REPORTED DRONE INTERCEPTIONS Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones. Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — a sharp increase from recent weeks when, on average, air defences took down 50% to 60%. Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defences struggling to cope with their speed. The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Zelenskiy said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot (missile interception) systems that can and must protect people's lives". Ukraine received a new €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defence needs, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said. The US-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles but tight global supplies have been drained by the Iran war as well as the Ukraine conflict. Russia's defence ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv. Last week Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an [USN:L1N45R056 TEXT:"interview"] with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow. PEOPLE SHELTER OVERNIGHT IN KYIV METRO Zelenskiy said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. In the Reuters interview, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure. Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's underground metro stations. Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night. "The metro is better because we live on the 9th floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the 9th floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters. Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles as well as the drones had targeted Kyiv. ($1 = 0.8947 euros)

item.title: Attacks on Saudi airports kill three people, as fighting escalates in Yemen
item.description: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports, the country's civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday, as fighting intensified in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray, Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports, the country's civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday, as fighting intensified in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces. One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, it said in a statement. One of the attacks was on Wednesday and the other on Tuesday, the civil aviation authorities said, without saying which attack had occurred on which day. The Saudi airport attacks were among a series of strikes targeting aviation infrastructure on Wednesday. Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden's international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones earlier on Wednesday, the country's Transport Ministry said. One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. The airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control. Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb Strait"], a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"launched a counteroffensive"] to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold. The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict , has revived a [USN:L6N45S0PX TEXT:"complex 12-year war"] in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country. The number of people displaced since the latest round of fighting began has risen to more than 200,000, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) [USN:L6N45T0PU TEXT:"said on Wednesday"]. "People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go," said IOM Director General Amy Pope, who called for more funding amid rising needs for food and shelter. Both sides allege that hundreds of people have been killed in fighting, without providing details. The UN says three in four families are going hungry in parts of Yemen. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, a US ally. On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. BATTLES OVER THE STRAIT Any Houthi control of the strait could threaten shipping or global oil flows, and Saudi Arabia has been seeking international assistance to repel the Houthis. Turkey is sending mainly [USN:L6N45T0IX TEXT:"defensive and technical support"], two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to implement a collective defence commitment under their [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"newly formed alliance"]. Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to ally Saudi Arabia amid the escalating war against the Houthis, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said. Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the people said. The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis. In response to a request for comment from the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war. Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government sources said. On Monday the Yemeni government said it had reached Mocha, which sits at a junction with a supply route to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim had been premature, according to Yemeni military officials on the ground and analysts. The Houthis, who control much of Yemen's north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran's influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations.

item.title: Euro drops toward 17-month lows, dollar holds gains after Fed minutes
item.description: The euro tumbled on Wednesday as French bonds came under renewed pressure on fiscal concerns, while the dollar held gains following the minutes from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak
item.content:encoded: The euro tumbled on Wednesday as French bonds came under renewed pressure on fiscal concerns, while the dollar held gains following the minutes from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting. Yields on [USN:L1N45T0KZ TEXT:"French and Italian debt rose"], with those of more indebted countries spiking more sharply than those of safe havens such as Germany as French fiscal worries dragged on and oil prices came back into focus. The French 10-year yield surged 11.9 basis points, on track for its biggest daily jump in two weeks, to 4.8696% while the German 10-year bond yield was unchanged at 3.4805%. "The case in Europe is that for a while they've operated a bit in a welfare-state type mode, spending a lot of money, not really bringing in a lot of revenue, and it's finally biting them. Considering also the fact that everybody has had to spend more money on energy, the outlook is not good," said Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington. "The focus is on Europe, and it's a very, very negative one." The euro slumped 0.53% to $1.1198, closing in on the 17-month lows hit on Monday. GREENBACK GAINS AHEAD OF FED MINUTES The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, was last up 0.32% to 102.24, briefly paring gains before recovering in the wake of the Fed minutes. The [USN:L6N45T0TQ TEXT:"minutes showed"] policymakers were divided last month over the rationale for raising interest rates, with "some participants" seeing a hike as needed to keep the impact of energy and other price shocks at bay, but a more hawkish core viewing it as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation. Recent comments from many Fed policymakers have been supportive of more rate hikes, although Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams and Vice Chair Philip Jefferson last week expressed a preference for patience in additional rate increases. The greenback was also supported as energy prices remain elevated, although oil prices [USN:L1N45T02U TEXT:"relinquished earlier gains"] in choppy trading after the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up a release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel in an effort to combat record high fuel prices. "We already kind of understand the dynamic that in a time when it's difficult to access energy resources, the US dollar is going to spike," said Perez. The chance of a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed's meeting later this month stands at 19.4%, from about 38% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch , but markets are pricing in an 83% chance of a hike at the Fed's December meeting. FRENCH DEBT UNDER PRESSURE Bond yields around the world have climbed in recent weeks due to expectations of central bank rate hikes as well as concerns about government finances. French debt is [USN:L6N45O0HP TEXT:"under growing pressure"] as politicians struggle to curb the budget deficit ahead of a divisive election in 2027. The calling of a [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election in Spain"] added to the pressure on the euro. France's economic situation is serious, given the rise in its borrowing costs, but the country does not at this point need help from the European Central Bank, Bank of France head [USN:L8N45T074 TEXT:"Emmanuel Moulin said"]. France will be "strategic" in its approach to issuing new debt, French Finance Minister [USN:L1N45T0OR TEXT:"Roland Lescure told"] the Wall Street Journal in an interview. "OATs (French bonds) do have room to sell off further, but I don't necessarily mean that it's going to be a panic. That's because France isn't yet hinting that it's close to default, so it's not yet getting to the point where we were having these conversations about Greece during the sovereign debt crisis," said Shriya Samarth, head of EMEA rates at StoneX. Sterling weakened 0.42% to $1.3216 against the greenback but hit its [USN:L6N45T0KZ TEXT:"highest level since"] June 2025 against the euro . Against the Japanese yen , the dollar weakened 0.09% to 157.95. The Bank of Japan's new policymaker, Ayano Sato, [USN:L1N45S130 TEXT:"said"][USN:L1N45S130 TEXT:" in an interview"] with the Kyodo news agency that she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages.

item.title: Oil prices settle down as IEA agrees to accelerate oil stock release
item.description: Oil prices settled lower on Wednesday following a choppy session after the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up a release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel in a bid to curb record-high fuel prices as the Iran war squeezes global supplies.
item.dc:creator: Georgina Mccartney
item.content:encoded: Oil prices settled lower on Wednesday following a choppy session after the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up a release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel in a bid to curb record-high fuel prices as the Iran war squeezes global supplies. Brent crude futures settled down 38 cents, or 0.38%, at $100.20 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled down $1.16, or 1.3%, to $88.28. The IEA said completing previously announced releases as quickly as possible could bring around 100 million barrels to market, although analysts and some governments said the figure did not necessarily represent a fresh intervention of that size. [USN:B5N44302B TEXT:"France"] will release 10 million barrels of diesel from its strategic stocks, Franceinfo radio reported on Wednesday, citing unnamed sources. "Europe is ground zero for this whole supply crunch ... and the releases address that and (take) some of the heat off the need for WTI to a degree. This should reduce some of the pressure on US supplies," said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital. Meanwhile, US crude stocks and distillate inventories fell while gasoline stocks rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said. Crude inventories fell by 3.2 million barrels to 424.1 million barrels in the week ended October 2, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.7 million-barrel rise. WAR RISKS TO SUPPLIES Investors are not convinced that recent rises in supply and exports from the Middle East are sustainable, PVM analyst Tamas Varga said, adding prices also drew support from the approaching US storm and the continuing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. Yemen's Houthis [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"attacked Aden international airport"] with missiles and drones, the country's transport ministry said, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Attacks in the Middle East have curbed Brent's losses compared with those of US crude futures, Kilduff said. US "requests and ideas" about Iran's nuclear program are [USN:S8N43Z008 TEXT:"at odds with"] Iranian demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters when asked about US Vice President JD Vance's comment that Iran must cut enrichment to end the war. Ukraine struck two Russian oil facilities while Russia [USN:L1N45T01B TEXT:"pounded Ukraine"] with waves of missiles and drones, killing at least 15 people, Ukrainian officials said. Strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and the loss of Middle East refining runs have [USN:L6N45S0MD TEXT:"tightened fuel"] markets, Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said on Tuesday. STORM HEADS TOWARD US PRODUCTION FACILITIES In the US, forecasters said on Tuesday that a [USN:L1N45S12U TEXT:"storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico"] would become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and is likely to hit oil and gas facilities. The US Gulf of Mexico produced 2.05 million barrels per day of crude oil in September, according to the EIA, accounting for around 15% of the country's total production. About 11.2 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates. The storm is an "unwelcome complication for crude, raising the prospect of production and refining disruptions at a time when the market already has enough supply-side headaches," KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said.

item.title: Former star US bond manager Leech fined by SEC, following guilty plea in 'cherry-picking' case
item.description: Kenneth Leech, the former star bond manager who pleaded guilty to obstructing a US Securities and Exchange Commission probe into alleged "cherry-picking," will pay a $3 million fine to settle the regulator's related civil case, the SEC said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Kenneth Leech, the former star bond manager who pleaded guilty to obstructing a US Securities and Exchange Commission probe into alleged "cherry-picking," will pay a $3 million fine to settle the regulator's related civil case, the SEC said on Tuesday. Leech's fine is in addition to the $100 million [USN:L6N42D0OE TEXT:"civil penalty"] that his former employer Western Asset Management Co, or Wamco, agreed to pay in June to resolve SEC civil charges it failed to properly supervise him "Cherry-picking" is the assigning of profitable trades to favored investors and losing trades to other investors. Authorities said Leech's alleged scheme involved more than $600 million and ran from January 2021 to October 2023 Tuesday's settlement requires court approval, and would result in $103 million being returned to harmed investors, the SEC said Leech and Wamco did not admit wrongdoing. Lawyers for Leech did not immediately respond to requests for comment Authorities accused Leech of waiting to see how trades performed on their first day before retroactively allocating them to clients, to boost Wamco revenue and his own compensation Leech allegedly steered better trades to "Macro Opportunities" portfolios that he said reflected his best ideas, and worse trades to "Core" and "Core Plus" portfolios Prosecutors accused Leech of lying during sworn SEC testimony by answering yes when asked if he had "an allocation in mind" when placing trades Leech pleaded guilty in June to one obstruction charge, and could face six to 12 months in prison under recommended federal sentencing guidelines. Prosecutors dropped four fraud charges Wamco is part of Franklin Resources (BEN.N) , whose brands include Franklin Templeton
